mcqs.question: 3Sum fixes an element at index i with an outer loop, then runs the opposite-end two-pointer pair search. What target does that inner search use?
options: target - arr[i]
target + arr[i]
arr[i] itself, ignoring the original target
The original target, unchanged
mcqs.explanation: Since arr[i] is already fixed as one of the three values, the remaining pair only needs to make up the rest of the sum — target minus the fixed value. Using the original target unchanged, or adding instead of subtracting, would search for the wrong pair entirely.

mcqs.question: In the duplicate-skipping 3Sum code, why do the left/right skip loops run only inside the branch where a match was just recorded, not before the sum is checked?
options: Running the skip loops before the sum check would raise an index-out-of-range error
A repeated value only becomes an unwanted duplicate once it's actually been used in a recorded triplet; skipping earlier would jump past triplets that haven't been tried yet
There is no difference; running the skips before or after the match check produces identical output
The skip loops must run before the sum check so left and right can converge correctly
mcqs.explanation: Adjacent equal values only need skipping to avoid re-recording the same triplet after one has already been found — skipping them proactively, before confirming a match, would incorrectly discard candidate values that were never actually part of an output triplet. Neither option raises an index error nor affects convergence on its own.

mcqs.question: Why must 3Sum's outer-loop duplicate skip be written as `if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]`, rather than dropping the `i > 0` guard?
options: Without the guard, comparing at i=0 reads nums[-1], the array's last element, producing wrong behavior on the very first iteration rather than an error
Without the guard, the loop throws an IndexError as soon as i reaches 0
The i > 0 guard is purely stylistic and has no effect on the output
The guard exists only to ensure the input array has at least three elements before looping
mcqs.explanation: Python allows negative indices, so nums[-1] is valid but wrong — it silently compares the first element against the last one instead of skipping nothing, corrupting behavior on the first iteration without ever raising an exception. It isn't a length check and isn't merely stylistic.

mcqs.question: Why does the 3Sum Closest solution skip the duplicate-triplet handling that plain 3Sum needs?
options: Because 3Sum Closest is only ever tested on arrays with no duplicate values
Because it tracks one running best-so-far value rather than collecting every distinct triplet, so re-encountering an equivalent triplet is harmless
Because sorting the array removes all duplicate values before the search begins
Because 3Sum Closest doesn't sort the array, so duplicate values are never adjacent
mcqs.explanation: Since the goal is a single closest sum rather than a list of distinct triplets, recomputing the same sum from a duplicate combination just re-evaluates the same candidate for 'best' — it costs nothing and changes nothing. The array is sorted here too, and sorting never removes duplicate values, only orders them.

mcqs.question: What's the fastest way to arrive at an efficient 3Sum solution if you already know the sorted-array pair-sum two-pointer technique?
options: Recognize 3Sum as pair-sum with one element fixed by an outer loop and subtracted from the target, repeated for every choice of fixed element
Start over and design a fresh hashmap-based approach built specifically for three values
Write three nested loops that check every possible triple directly against the target
Apply the pair-sum two-pointer technique three separate times on non-overlapping thirds of the array
mcqs.explanation: 3Sum is structurally pair-sum wrapped in one outer loop — recognizing that reuses the already-proven O(n) convergence argument instead of re-deriving it, arriving directly at O(n²). The nested-triple-loop approach is the O(n³) brute force this pattern is meant to avoid, and splitting the array into thirds doesn't correspond to how triplets are actually distributed across it.
